title: Kierkegaard's individual
hookLine: each person stands before God alone, not as part of a crowd

cards: A stadium rises to its feet before anyone has decided anything. A group chat piles onto someone, and it's oddly easy to add one more laughing face. A crowd can carry a person a long way without asking a single question.

In Copenhagen, Søren Kierkegaard, the Danish writer this path met earlier, watched this happen in the newspapers, in the streets, and, he thought, in the churches too. So he did something odd for an author.
He dedicated some of his books not to a crowd of readers, but to one: that single individual, whoever you are, reading alone.

teach.b: His sharp sentence for it is usually put in English as: the crowd is untruth. He didn't mean people in groups are bad.

He meant a crowd lets each person hide. In a crowd nobody quite decides; everyone goes along, and nobody quite answers for it. Against the crowd he set a picture from the Bible: each person standing before God, alone.
Paul writes to the Romans: "So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God." Every one. Of himself.
Not as a member of a nation, a family, or even a congregation.
In Fear and Trembling he dwells on Abraham on the mountain, called by name, and answering, "Here am I." No committee. One voice, one answer.
Kierkegaard wasn't against church or neighbors; he wrote a whole book, Works of Love, about loving the neighbor. His point was that nobody can hold your faith for you.
Growing up in a country that called itself Christian, he thought, didn't make anyone a Christian by itself; each person had to become one, with their own yes. Some Christians find this bracing.
Others worry it leaves too little room for the church as one body, and point out how often scripture says "we." Both readings are alive today.
But the picture he left is hard to shake: before God, there's no back row to hide in.

how: Christians shaped by Kierkegaard often stress personal decision and honest self-examination before God, alongside life in a church; his books are read by Protestants, Catholics and readers of no faith.

games.q: the whole room is nodding along to something you're not sure is true. what does Kierkegaard's individual do?
o: nod too; the crowd is probably right.
stop, and answer for yourself, as before God.
walk out and never join anything again.
games.why: the crowd is untruth, he said, because it lets each person hide. but he also wrote Works of Love: the point is standing on your own feet, not leaving people.

practice: Bring to mind a small choice that's been waiting, a call to return, an invitation to answer, a habit you keep mostly because everyone around you does, and set aside for a moment what the group would say.
What do you think: not the loudest answer, but yours? If you pray, you can bring it before God with Abraham's answer: here am I.

wordCard.voice: Kierkegaard's individual. The Danish writer's picture of each person standing before God alone: answerable, seen, not hidden in a crowd.
